name: Bradley Reaves
affiliation: Associate Professor, North Carolina State University
title: Let's End Phone Spam with NextG
abstract: While advanced data connectivity remains a focus of mobile network design, individuals and organizations still rely heavily on traditional voice and text messaging. Despite long running efforts, these channels remain clogged with spam that costs millions in losses and the inner tranquility of every phone user. In this talk, we'll explore the root causes that allow this abuse to continue, why prior efforts to stop it have failed, and conclude with hopeful optimism on the role NextG can play in more trustworthy communications.
bio: Brad Reaves is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer Science at NC State University and a member of the Wolfpack Security and Privacy Research (WSPR) Lab. His research focuses on measuring and improving the security and privacy of computer systems, with particular emphasis on telephone networks and mobile platforms. Reaves' work spans topics such as mobile malware detection, fraud in mobile money systems, and techniques to differentiate between legitimate and fraudulent phone calls. His interdisciplinary research integrates concepts from signal processing, digital communications, data science, machine learning, statistics, cryptography, program analysis, reverse engineering, and network security. He regularly collaborates with students and researchers to address real-world threats and develop practical security solutions that impact both users and systems at scale.

name: Endadul Hoque
title: Fuzzing with Context: Rethinking Security Testing for Modern Systems
abstract: Fuzzing is a cornerstone of automated security testing, discovering vulnerabilities by feeding programs malformed or unexpected inputs. While general-purpose fuzzers have uncovered many bugs in real-world systems, they struggle to exercise deeper program logic, as they fail to generate context-sensitive inputs that satisfy the semantic and structural constraints required to traverse deeper execution paths. Such context sensitivity is pervasive in modern systems: protocol specifications encode intricate relationships between fields, cryptographic libraries enforce strict requirements, and operating system kernels expose system call interfaces dependent on rich, evolving state. These constraints fundamentally limit conventional fuzzing approaches that lack semantic awareness. In this talk, I will present our experiences and lessons learned in advancing fuzzing techniques to address these challenges. First, I will show the limitations of traditional fuzzers in testing protocol implementations, based on a systematic study of their effectiveness when confronted with context-sensitive input requirements. Next, I will turn to system software, highlighting how context sensitivity manifests at the system call interface of the Linux kernel and why existing kernel fuzzers fall short. I will introduce a novel approach that leverages large language models to generate context-aware C programs, enabling more effective exploration of kernel behavior. Finally, I will discuss our comparative study on the role of language models in fuzzing, evaluating their effectiveness as assistants to general-purpose fuzzers versus specialized, domain-specific fuzzing techniques for cryptographic primitives.
bio: Endadul Hoque is an Assistant Professor at Syracuse University (SU) in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. His research broadly focuses on the security of computer networks and systems, with an emphasis on automated vulnerability detection, applied program analysis, and building resilient systems. Prior to joining SU, he was an Assistant Professor at Florida International University (FIU) and a Postdoctoral Research Associate at Northeastern University. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Purdue University. He received two Best Paper Awards (NDSS 2018, SBFT 2025), a Google Research Scholar Award (2022), and a NSF CAREER Award (2024).

name: Farbod Tavakkoli
title: OTel: A GPU-Agnostic Open Stack for Telecom AI
abstract: Telecom is a hard domain for general-purpose LLMs and an underserved one for open AI infrastructure. OTel (Open Telco AI) tackles both: curated open datasets, 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines covering retrieval, reranking, and generation, and a GPU-agnostic training pipeline that runs on both AMD and NVIDIA hardware. I'll walk through the data curation, training recipe, and held-out evaluation behind the release and share lessons from a project that has surpassed 16 million downloads and 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide.
bio: Farbod is a Data Scientist at AT&T and the technical lead of the Open Telco AI project (OTel), an open-source initiative delivering curated telecom datasets and a family of telecom-specialized language, embedding, and reranking models. The released OTel models have surpassed 16 million downloads and received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. His work focuses on training and deploying domain-specific large language models at scale across both AMD and NVIDIA hardware, spanning the full generative AI lifecycle from data curation and model design to evaluation, benchmarking, deployment, and open-source release. He has also contributed to modern LLM benchmarks including GSMA, Spider 2.0, and BIRD. More broadly, his background spans engineering and applied research across transportation safety, healthcare, climate and environmental analytics, housing stability, and social equity.
